lesson.title: Think the N
lesson.subtitle: The four nasal vowels: on, en, an, in — the sound of not arriving

hook.title: The Sound of Not Saying
hook.content: French's most foreign sound is an absence. In pain (bread), vingt (twenty), bon (good), on (we), the N is written and never pronounced — but you must still think it. The vowel leans toward the N and stops: that lean IS the nasal vowel. We don't 'drop' the N; we don't arrive at it.

footnotes.title: Why French did this
footnotes.content: Latin vowels before N/M swallowed the consonant into the vowel itself: panem → pain, bonum → bon. The consonant became breath. English did it too — once: think of the 'nasal' in 'sing', where the G is written and not said.

pattern.title: Four Colors of Not-Arriving
pattern.content: on /ɔ̃/ as in bon, mon — the mouth rounds and hums. an/en /ɑ̃/ as in pain's cousin enfant, très bien's bien — the mouth opens low. in/ain /ɛ̃/ as in pain, vin, main — the mouth spreads. (The fourth, un /œ̃/, is merging with in for most speakers.) Same technique for all: shape the vowel, start toward the N, stop.

footnotes.title: The test word
footnotes.content: Say 'singing' in English — the final -ing where the G never lands. That unfinished feeling is the nasal vowel. French just does it in four colors.

pattern.trap_note: Don't actually say the N: pain said with a hard N becomes 'pen' and nobody hears bread. The N is a direction, not a destination.

exercises.prompt: Match each nasal word with its meaning:
exercises.explanation: All four wear a silent N — and all four lean into it.

exercises.prompt: Which word does NOT have a nasal vowel?
exercises.explanation: rouge's /ʒ/ is a full consonant. pain, bonjour (bon+jour), vin all lean toward a silent N.

exercises.prompt: Pronunciation map: which syllable contains the nasal vowel in 'bonjour'?
exercises.meaning: the nasal vowel is inside bon- — and the N never lands
exercises.explanation: bon /bɔ̃/ + jour /ʒuʁ/. The first syllable hums; the second is clean.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the two-nasal sentence: 'The bread is good'
exercises.explanation: pain (/pɛ̃/) and bon (/bɔ̃/) both lean toward a silent N without landing on it.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: pain — the ɛ̃ nasal: spread the mouth, don't land on the N
bon — the ɔ̃ nasal: round and hum
exercises.explanation: Two nasals guarding one clean est between them.
exercises.affirmation: Both Ns were directions, not destinations — that's the whole clinic.

summary.outcome: Produce the four nasal vowels by leaning toward the N without arriving — in pain, vingt, bon, on.

use_example.german: Le pain est bon, on y va.
use_example.english: The bread is good — shall we?

summary.takeaway: The N is a direction, not a destination. Unfinished is correct.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5031] Actuellement, Librairie & Co.): see how Think the N leads directly into Actuellement, Librairie & Co..

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "The bread is good" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Le pain est bon" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Think the N.

pain.etymology_derivation: Latin pānis 'bread' — a pantry is literally the bread-room. The N is thought, not said: the nasal vowel is the lesson.

vingt.etymology_derivation: Latin vīgintī — English 'vigesimal' (counting by twenties) is the same root; French just kept counting that way: quatre-vingts.

bon.etymology_derivation: Latin bonus 'good' — English borrowed the word back as 'bonus', a good thing added.

on.context_translation: Shall we go to the café?
on.etymology_derivation: on is worn-down homme — 'the man says' became 'one says' became spoken French's everyday 'we'. The nasal vowel is the fossil.

ne.etymology_derivation: Latin nōn wore down to ne. The verb sits in a ne...pas sandwich; spoken French often drops the first slice.
